To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

caffeine inhibits adenosine receptors in the cerebral circulation, and that this blockade of adenosine receptors may be responsible, at least in part, for the vasoconstrictor effect of caffeine on cerebral arteries.

caffeine, by blocking adenosine A1 and A2B receptors, inhibits the neurovascular coupling mechanism and that chronic caffeine exposure may alter the sensitivity of cerebral vascular smooth muscle to the vasodilatory effects of adenosine.
caffeine, through inhibition of adenosine A1, A1, and A2A receptors, interferes with the neurovascular coupling process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how changes in the activity of adenosine receptors, and the subsequent changes in the release of neurotransmitters, such as nitric oxide, may affect the regulation of cerebral vascular tone.
the role that adenosine receptors play in the regulation of cerebral blood flow, and with the effects of caffeine on those receptors

the influence of caffeine and other adenosine receptor antagonists on the regulation of cerebrovascular function, with an emphasis on the mechanisms by which adenosine receptors, particularly those located on the cerebrovasculature, may be linked to changes in cerebral hemodynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
caffeine, through the blockade of adenosine receptors, may interfere, at least in part, in the regulation of the cerebral circulation.
the effects of caffeine on cerebral blood flow (CBF) regulation are complex and not fully understood.

caffeine influences cerebral hemodynamics through a number of mechanisms, some of which are not well understood and may differ depending on the dose, duration, and route of administration of this drug.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of acute and chronic caffeine intake on the cerebral circulation are not identical and, in fact, may be diametrically opposed.

caffeine, through its actions on adenosine receptor-mediated processes, has the potential to influence cerebral vascular regulation, and that such influence may depend on the duration of caffeine exposure.
caffeine, in its ability to block adenosine receptors, can influence cerebral vascular tone and, thus, blood flow, and this influence can vary with the duration of exposure to the drug.
The main takeaway from our work is that
caffeine has a complex, multifaceted influence on cerebral hemodynamics.
the acute administration of caffeine, at doses that are within the range of those consumed by humans, is associated with a significant reduction in cerebrovascular tone.
, while caffeine has a number of potential targets, the major influence of caffeine on cerebral hemodynamics is through blockade of adenosine A1 and A2A receptors.
